title: TODO.md — punch list
text:
Always check TODO.md before starting work. Update it as tasks land ([x]), start ([~]), or get skipped ([-]). See LOG.md for the history behind any line, METHODOLOGY.md for the data/scope rules, and PLAN.md for the full phased build order.



Remove the nested rva-sourcebook/ duplicate subfolder (superseded by root files).
Remove stale generic scaffold: rva-sourcebook.qmd, app.R, _site/.
Rewrite PLAN.md — was a Fauquier County/Better Housing Coalition plan for an unrelated engagement.
Rewrite CLAUDE.md — fix geography section (rr/bhc/secondary/ashland/regions, not pha/4-primary), switch book → website language, drop PHA/BHC client-review conventions, add mapgl section, trim “Known gotchas” to what’s real.
Reset this file to a real, accurate punch list.
Write README.md (quick start, renv guide, status).
Write METHODOLOGY.md (geography/scope conventions, referenced by CLAUDE.md but never written).
Reconcile _quarto.yml — real navbar (Home/About/Inventory/Demographics/Market/Data Notes), output-dir: docs, freeze: auto, execute-dir: project. Added stub content to inventory.qmd/demographics.qmd/market.qmd/data-notes.qmd/index.qmd/about.qmd so the site renders end-to-end even before real data lands.
First LOG.md entry for this session.
Commit the cleanup (including removing the leftover rva-sourcebook/ folder that survived the first pass).





renv::init() + renv::snapshot() — user runs, package installs are a long job. Pin R + tidyverse/tidycensus/tigris/sf/mapgl/kableExtra/ggtext/formattable/janitor.
Add .Rprofile (source("renv/activate.R")) once renv exists.
renv::snapshot() 2026-11-12 recorded arrow, assertthat, readxlsb (GitHub source velofrog/readxlsb, compiled; needs Rtools to restore). renv::status() clean.
Define a palette + light theme in _common.R — rva_pal (8-hue categorical), rva_seq (sequential blue ramp), rva_ink (chart chrome), theme_rva(). Values from the dataviz skill’s validated reference palette.
Decide the mapgl basemap style — rva_map_style in _common.R, Carto’s free Positron MapLibre style, no token.
r/geo.R written — tigris county/independent-city boundaries for the rr region → data/geo.rds + data-out/geo.csv.
Run Rscript r/geo.R — user runs (tigris pull is a long job). Confirms data/geo.rds writes clean and the validation block passes (17 localities, valid geometry, EPSG:4326). Verified 2026-09-16: data/geo.rds is an sf frame, 17 rows, all rr GEOIDs, EPSG:4326, zero empty geometries.
Confirm CENSUS_API_KEY is visible (Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != "") — TRUE/FALSE check only, never print the value. Not needed by geo.R (tigris doesn’t require a key) but will be for every ACS script from Phase 2 on. Verified TRUE 2026-09-16 via the .Renviron fallback.
[-] Once mapgl is in renv.lock, build one small proof-of-concept map (e.g. rr region colored by aland) to confirm rva_map_style + data/geo.rds actually render before wiring real data into it. Blocked: mapgl is not in renv.lock — needs a user-run renv::install("mapgl") + renv::snapshot().
r/acs_tenure.R’s header comment (lines 18–21) still says “8 rr localities” / “4 primary localities” / region4 — doesn’t match _common.R (rr=17, bhc=3) or the script’s own region3 pooling. Sibling-project debris missed in the 2026-09-15 cleanup; reconcile the comment (and sanity-check no other r/*.R header has the same mismatch).





r/acs_stock.R — ACS B25001 (units), B25002/B25004 (occupancy/vacancy), B25024 (structure type), B25034–36 (year built). Ran clean; validation passes. B25036 dropped from scope — not published in the 2014 window, which would break the three-window trend (recorded in METHODOLOGY.md). B25035 is pulled but carries no pooled rows, since a median can’t be summed.
BPS building permits (census.gov text files) — annual permits by structure type for the rr region. r/bps_permits.R, 2000–2025, cached under data/cache/bps/. Ran clean; the rr17 pooled row reconciles to its 17 members in all 26 years.
Build out inventory.qmd (currently an empty stub). 6 figures, 3 tables, takeaway H2s, bullets, callouts; renders standalone in ~10s.





r/acs_demographics.R written and run 2026-10-28 (population + age/sex B01001, race/ethnicity B03002, household type B11001, income B19001/B19013/B25118; 3 windows, 25 geographies incl. pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17). User confirmed validation passed.
Build out demographics.qmd — 7 figures, 3 tables, takeaway H2s, computed-inline bullets, reliability + race-coding callouts. Rendered standalone 2026-10-28 and figures checked visually. All 7 fig- chunks have fig-alt. (Bullet figures are computed inline; the fig-alt text carries typed rounded numbers that will drift on a data refresh, same as inventory.qmd.)
r/pep_migration.R + migration sections in demographics.qmd (added 2026-10-28 at the user’s request, not in the original plan). PEP components of change (natural, international, domestic migration) for the 17 localities, pooled core/ring/region, and Virginia, 2010–2019 and 2020–2025. Ran clean; validation passes, including a same-vintage match to the Census API for all 17 localities. 4 figures, 1 table, 1 callout, all fig-alt present; rendered and checked.





acs_burden.R reviewed 2026-10-28. Its output was not current — data/acs_burden.rds never existed. Fixed before first run: dropped the sibling-project tract tier and baseline_2022 block, fixed stale acs_income.R refs, switched the collapsed-band MOE to quadrature (was moe_sum(moe, estimate) on an already-summed scalar), added pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17 rows, rewrote the validation block (25 geographies × 3 windows × 2 tenures × 4 categories; rr17 reconciles to its 17 members). User ran it; validation passed.
[~] r/bls_wage.R written (BLS LAUS unemployment + CES average hourly earnings + CPI-U, Richmond MSA vs. regions metros) — not yet run. User: renv::install("blscrapeR") + renv::snapshot(), confirm BLS_KEY is in .Renviron, then Rscript r/bls_wage.R and paste back the validation output. Check that the three comparison metros’ CES wage series came back (a warning names any that didn’t).
Add a bls_cap() caption helper to _common.R when the market page first charts bls_wage.rds (oews_cap/cpi_cap don’t fit — cpi_cap says “via FRED”).
[~] r/acs_market.R written 2026-10-28 — B25003 tenure (not covered by acs_tenure.R, which is race-specific only), B25077 home value, B25064 rent; medians carry nominal + real columns. Not yet run — user: Rscript r/acs_market.R, paste back validation output.
[~] market.qmd drafted 2026-10-28 (7 figures, 4 tables, callouts; replaces the old book’s split ownership.qmd/rental.qmd). Code and layout verified against a scratchpad mock acs_market.rds (real B25118 tenure counts, synthetic medians) — the real render is blocked on the user running Rscript r/acs_market.R and pasting back validation output. After that: render market.qmd for real, re-read every figure, and revisit the three flagged items — the “Home values and rents climbed in every core locality” H2, the “Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest” H2, and the fig-alt text on fig-value/fig-rent/fig-pti/fig-rent-share, all written before the home-value and rent data existed.





r/pums/pums_profiles.R — tidy household/resident estimates by AMI band × tenure × geography with replicate-weight SEs and reliability flags → data/pums_profiles.rds, data-out/pums_ami_dist.csv, data-out/pums_profile.csv. Ran clean; PUMS owner/renter households in the core-3 PUMAs match ACS B25003 within 0.6%.
profiles.qmd — 11 figures, 3 tables, takeaway H2s, computed-inline bullets, geography + reliability callouts; every fig- chunk has fig-alt. Added to the navbar.
summary.qmd — executive summary of inventory, demographics, market; now includes an income-band section drawn from profiles.qmd. Added to the navbar.
inventory.qmd bullet “peaked at [2022’s 10,414] … a 76% collapse” is wrong: 2022 is the series high and the pre-crash peak was ~8,400 (2005). Its “multifamily first exceeded single-family in 2022” line also needs a check (2024 was single-family-led). summary.qmd words it around the error.
r/pums/pums_prep.R runs (2026-10-30, after the user added naics_soc_lookup.R and data-out/puma_pow.csv) and writes data/pums_rva.rds (48,802 persons, 215 columns). Nothing reads it yet. Still no script header block.
r/pums/*.R don’t follow the script anatomy (no header block, no source("_common.R"), pums_ami.R ends with an unguarded ggplot() call). pums_ami.R also hardcodes the HUD CSV path (data/summary_county_5176099999.csv) and the CPI factor; data/ is gitignored, so the HUD file isn’t in the repo — note where it came from in data-notes.qmd.
r/pums/ is untracked in git; commit it with profiles.qmd, summary.qmd, and the log.
data-notes.qmd needs a PUMS / AMI section (geography caveat, FY2026 limits, CPI inflation, replicate-weight SEs). See METHODOLOGY.md.
Optional: a mapgl choropleth of share at/below 80% AMI by PUMA for Phase 5 (boundaries for all PUMAs are in data/puma_va.rds; the profiles now cover the seven core-three PUMAs).





r/evict.R — combines the three data-out/*-virginia-filings.csv exports (Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield) into data/evict.rds (monthly, annual, summary) + data-out/evict_monthly.csv, evict_annual.csv. Ran clean; validation passes.
“Eviction filings” section in market.qmd (2 figures, 1 table, bullets, caveat callout, bullet in the opening tip box). Renders clean.
Eviction section added to summary.qmd (2026-11-03).
Add an eviction paragraph to data-notes.qmd (source, baseline definition, partial 2026).
Confirm the source and the “historical average” baseline definition; the exports don’t document either.





r/hmda_prep.R — core-three, principal-residence, 1-4 unit; originations, denial rates (locality, purpose, race/ethnicity), denial reasons → data/hmda.rds + data-out/hmda_*.csv.
Lending section in market.qmd (2 figures, 1 table, bullets, callout) and a bullet in the opening box.
r/hmda.R has no header/validation, no source("_common.R") (uses rr), and leaves four stray all(is.na(...)) lines on columns that aren’t selected; bring to script anatomy.
Lending added to summary.qmd (2026-11-03).
Add lending to data-notes.qmd (denial-rate definition, HMDA coverage).





summary.qmd section “For external affairs: connecting the data to Better Housing Coalition’s work”: quotable-numbers table, bullets by BHC line of work (rental, senior, homeownership, mixed-income/mixed-use), and a “using these figures” callout.
r/summary_audit.R -> data/summary_audit.rds + data-out/summary_audit.csv: 90% MOEs and independent HMDA/eviction re-computation for the figures the BHC section quotes (2026-11-03). Re-run after any data refresh; the page reads it.
Re-check summary.qmd’s hand-typed numbers (none remain in prose, but the Profiles and market fig-alt text carries rounded values).
BHC to supply program facts (units, residents served, pipeline) to pair with the regional figures; the section deliberately states none beyond the 8 senior properties.
Mixed-use has no direct data (retail/commercial demand); consider a public source if this section is used for that case.





One mapgl choropleth per page (e.g. inventory: vacancy rate by locality; demographics: median household income; market: median rent or home value).





data-notes.qmd — public-facing methodology, derived from METHODOLOGY.md.
about.qmd — real content (currently a one-line stub).
Full quarto render completes with no errors.
Every #| label: fig- chunk has a matching #| fig-alt: line. (inventory.qmd is done — 6 of 6.)
GitHub Pages live from docs/ on main.





cache_table = TRUE is deprecated in current tidycensus (one warning per get_acs() call, ignored). CLAUDE.md still prescribes it. Drop it project-wide in one pass — acs_stock.R, acs_tenure.R, acs_burden.R, and the CLAUDE.md line together — rather than piecemeal.
theme_rva()‘s caption switched to element_textbox_simple() so long source lines wrap instead of clipping. The other pages’ charts haven’t been re-rendered against it yet; check them when Phases 3–4 land.
formattable::comma()/percent() mask the scales versions (_common.R loads formattable last) and take digits, not accuracy. inventory.qmd works around it with local n_fmt()/p_fmt() wrappers — consider promoting those to _common.R before the next page repeats the workaround.





presentation.qmd + presentation.css — 10-slide reveal.js deck built from the summary.qmd findings (BHC section first): headline on every slide, big-number cards plus charts, a six-figure quotables table with margins of error, a cautions slide for Q&A. Speaker notes on each slide. Renders standalone to docs/presentation.html.
Deck linked from the site navbar (Presentation tab, opens in a new tab), 2026-11-12. Not committed yet.
Six 2027 General Assembly legislation slides added 2026-11-12 (nine LIS bills plus unfiled proposals).
Legislation slides: confirm the unfiled proposals’ source can be shown publicly; add patrons and bill numbers once filed; refresh LIS statuses before the session opens (snapshot is 2026-11-12). Read the LIS history for HB143, HB1376 and SB349 if the slides should say whether they were carried over.
Setup chunk copies a subset of summary.qmd’s helpers; if those change (or get promoted to _common.R), update the deck too. (Renter-income helpers now exist in summary.qmd, presentation.qmd and demographics.qmd — a strong case for promoting inc_renter() to _common.R.)
BHC branding on the site and the deck (_brand.yml, styles.css, presentation.css, navbar logo, favicon, title-slide logo).
Confirm brand blue/red/brown against the brand guide (extracted only as CMYK swatches, converted approximately) and the logo usage rules; update _brand.yml and rva_brand in _common.R together.
Optional: Lato in R charts (showtext/sysfonts); charts currently use the system sans font.
Before publishing docs/: confirm BHC has cleared use of its logo and brand on the public site. img/ logo files are still untracked.




Why: the question is whether renters can move to ownership, so home values and rents are compared with median renter household income (ACS B25119), not the all-household median.

r/acs_demographics.R pulls B25119 (median_income_renter; nominal + real, 3 windows, all geographies) → data/acs_demographics.rds, data-out/acs_demographics.csv.
r/summary_audit.R has pti_* (renter denominator) and renter_income_real_chg keys.
presentation.qmd: price-vs-income chart, homeownership stat, and quotables use renter income.
summary.qmd: pti()/rent_share() and every income comparison switched to renter income; renter row in the at-a-glance table; all-household income kept as a reference figure.
market.qmd: renter-income versions of the price-to-income and rent-share figures (fig-pti-renter, fig-rent-share-renter); the all-household versions stay.
demographics.qmd: renter median-income figure (fig-income-renter) and bullets.
User: Rscript r/summary_audit.R — the 2026-11-03 audit files predate B25119, so au("pti_2024") still shows the all-household margin and au("renter_income_real_chg") is empty until it re-runs. Then paste back the output.
Quoted-figure review: senior sample size (509, not 50), eviction wording, “two-thirds” seniors claim (2026-11-12). Direct senior counts added to pums_profiles.R.
pums_profiles.R and summary_audit.R re-run with direct senior counts (2026-11-12).
User: render summary and presentation (they now read P$seniors).
User: render demographics, market, summary, presentation and re-read the new figures. Not yet rendered; market.qmd and demographics.qmd are frozen pages, so confirm they actually re-execute.
Check the typed numbers in the new fig-alt text (renter ratio ~5.9 to ~6.5; renter income ~$38k to ~$48k for Richmond city, ~$48k to ~$55k for the metro) against the rendered figures.
Add B25119 and the renter-income rationale to data-notes.qmd and METHODOLOGY.md (median of renter-occupied households; B25119 is published in all three windows).
Confirm B25119 estimate_real for small localities: renter-income cells for Amelia (CV 43) and similar are Low reliability and should be suppressed anywhere they’re tabled.





r/chesterfield_pay.R, r/chesterfield_afford.R, chesterfield-onepager.qmd (HTML + one-page Typst PDF), navbar entry, data-notes paragraph. Spec and plan in design/.
2026-11-24: restyled from the BHC Brand Identity Guide and added cost burden, AMI mix, seniors, household size/bedrooms and growth panels (r/chesterfield_context.R, fonts/, rva_guide in _common.R).
Reconcile _brand.yml, styles.css and rva_brand with the guide’s palette (orange #E86C1F, amber #FBB035, cream #FEE49B, green #8CC63F, sky #ADE0ED, teal #00617F); the current blue/red/brown are CMYK guesses not in the guide.
Check the HTML version of the one-pager in a browser (not visually checked 2026-11-24).
Optional: CHAS-based senior and small-household need; the page uses ACS.
Confirm the adopted FY27 CCPS pay (teacher $57,277, instructional assistant $17.81/hr, bus driver $25.11/hr were proposed in Feb 2026). If adopted: mark the old FY26 teacher and bus rows stale, mark the FY27 rows current in r/chesterfield_pay.R (the script now fails if a role has two current rows), re-run both scripts, then re-render chesterfield-onepager.qmd.
Deputy sheriff pay ($56,741) is from a January 2026 posting; re-check against the current posting or pay plan.
Source or replace the unsourced insurance (0.35%) and PMI (0.7%) assumptions in r/chesterfield_afford.R.
Confirm BHC has cleared its logo on the public PDF; decide whether the page needs an “ask” line (needs BHC’s position).
The public safety pay-plan step table was not found; add mid-career pay if it is published.
User: full quarto render — the navbar changed on every page, and docs/ for the other pages is stale.





PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar, vulnerable-populations data. The PUMA geography groundwork (puma_core3/puma_region/puma_locality) already exists in _common.R if this ever gets picked up — see METHODOLOGY.md.

section: Richmond city has the highest share of lower-income households, but most lower-income renters live in Henrico and Chesterfield
text:
Richmond city has the highest share of lower-income households, but most lower-income renters live in Henrico and Chesterfield








Figure 3






50.9% of Richmond city households earn 80% of AMI or less, against 39.1% in Henrico and 33.4% in Chesterfield.
The city’s lead holds within each tenure: 64.3% of its renters and 33.9% of its owners are at 80% of AMI or less.

title: Profiles
section: Cost burden falls steeply with income, and low-income renters carry the most
text:
Cost burden falls steeply with income, and low-income renters carry the most








Figure 4






Among households at 30% of AMI or less, 80.8% of renters and 67.2% of owners pay half or more of income on housing.
Burden falls with each band: renters go from 90.1% cost-burdened (30%+) in the lowest band to 62.0% at 51-80% of AMI and 3.2% above 120%; owners go from 83.2% to 39.4% to 2.4%.
The renter-owner gap is widest at 31-50% of AMI, where 87.0% of renters are cost-burdened against 57.6% of owners (29 points); by 81-120% of AMI the two are within 2 points.
Owner costs include mortgage, taxes, insurance, and utilities; renter costs are gross rent.

title: Profiles
section: Household makeup shifts from people living alone to couples as income rises
text:
Household makeup shifts from people living alone to couples as income rises








Figure 5






Living alone is the most common household type in the lowest band for both tenures: 58.5% of renters and 59.6% of owners.
Single-parent households are 19.4% of renters at 30% of AMI or less, against 4.5% above 120%.
Couples with children are 30.4% of owners above 120% of AMI and 4.9% of owners at 30% or less.









Figure 6






No household member earns $5,000 or more in 71.1% of owners and 58.3% of renters at 30% of AMI or less.
At the other end, 63.6% of owners and 63.0% of renters above 120% of AMI have two or more earners.
Most renters at 31-50% of AMI (63.9%) have exactly one earner.
37.6% of renter households and 35.3% of owner households at 30% of AMI or less include a member with a disability, against 19.4% and 18.9% above 120%.

Owners in the lowest bands are older; renters are younger at every income level

The median householder is 66 for owners at 30% of AMI or less and 52 above 120%; for renters the medians are 45 and 39.
52.9% of the lowest-income owners are 65 or over — typically a retired homeowner on a fixed income.
Renters aged under 35 are 44.2% of the 51-80% band and 43.9% of the 81-120% band.









Figure 8






Black householders are 55.9% of renters at 30% of AMI or less and 23.1% of renters above 120%.
Among owners the same gradient runs from 39.1% at 30% or less to 16.7% above 120%.
White non-Hispanic householders are 69.9% of owners above 120% of AMI.
Hispanic or Latino householders are 12.8% of renters at 31-50% of AMI, their largest share among renter bands.









Figure 9






Single-family detached homes house 81.6% of owners at 30% of AMI or less and 90.3% of owners above 120%.
Renters at 30% of AMI or less live in buildings of 2 or more units at a rate of 72.6%; above 120% the share is 56.2%.
43.4% of renters above 120% of AMI live in single-family homes, against 26.5% of renters at 30% or less.

People 65 and over are 35.7% of residents in the lowest-income owner households, against 13.9% above 120% of AMI.

Reliability of the profile cells



Counts and medians in every band are high-reliability. Shares are noisier where a category is small: of the 459 category-by-band-by-tenure shares estimated, 54 are medium-reliability (CV 15-30) and 9 are low-reliability (CV above 30). Tables suppress low-reliability cells (—) and mark medium ones (*); the stacked bars show every estimate, and a very thin segment should not be read as a precise number. title: PLAN.md — RVA Sourcebook build plan
text:
This is a personal/portfolio project, not a client deliverable. It’s a public Quarto website covering basic Richmond-region housing data — inventory, demographics, and market — sourced entirely from public data (Census/ACS, BLS), with ggplot2 static charts and mapgl interactive maps. See CLAUDE.md for session conventions, TODO.md for the punch list, and METHODOLOGY.md for geography/scope details.


Earlier drafts of this repo’s docs (CLAUDE.md, TODO.md, and a prior PLAN.md) were copy-pasted from two unrelated sibling engagements — a Richmond-nonprofit regional report with a much larger scope (PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar pipelines) and a wholly separate Fauquier County study — and never reconciled to this project’s actual geography or scope. _common.R and r/acs_tenure.R / r/acs_burden.R are the real, working foundation; everything else was rebuilt from scratch on 2026-09-15 to match. If you find a stray reference to PHA, BHC-as-client, Fauquier, or a script under r/pums/, r/chas.R, r/mls_* that doesn’t exist in this repo — it’s leftover from that history. Flag it.



In scope (v1): - Inventory — housing stock, occupancy/vacancy, structure type, year built, building permits. - Demographics — population, age/sex, race/ethnicity, household composition, income. - Market — tenure, home values, rents, cost burden.
All from public sources: tidycensus (ACS, decennial, PEP), tigris (boundaries), BLS (OEWS/QCEW where useful), Census BPS permits.
Out of scope for now: PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar, vulnerable-populations data. The PUMA geography groundwork (puma_core3, puma_region, puma_locality in _common.R) already exists from the earlier copy-paste and is harmless to keep, but nothing is built toward it yet.

Quarto website (not book) — _quarto.yml type website, output to docs/ for GitHub Pages, freeze: auto, execute-dir: project. Pages: Home (index.qmd), About (about.qmd), Inventory (inventory.qmd), Demographics (demographics.qmd), Market (market.qmd), Data Notes (data-notes.qmd).



mapgl for interactive choropleths and point maps, backed by a free MapLibre basemap style (Carto or ESRI — no Mapbox token needed). Boundary data comes from r/geo.R → data/geo.rds, joined to whatever ACS/permit table a given map needs. Static ggplot2 remains the default for everything that isn’t inherently spatial.

title: Market
section: Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest
text:
Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest









Figure 4






In the Richmond MSA the typical home was worth 4.1 times the typical household income in the 2024 window, against 3.6 times in the 2014 window.
Among the core three, the ratio is 5.5 in Richmond city, 4.0 in Henrico, and 3.6 in Chesterfield; statewide it is 4.1.









Figure 5






Measured against renter households, the typical Richmond MSA home was worth 6.5 times the typical renter income in the 2024 window, against 5.9 times in the 2014 window.
Among the core three, the renter ratio is 7.3 in Richmond city, 6.0 in Henrico, and 5.9 in Chesterfield; statewide it is 6.4.
This is the more relevant gap for renters weighing a move to ownership, but it is still a ratio of two medians: it does not say how many renters could qualify for a loan.









Figure 6






Annual median rent equals 25.5% of Richmond city’s median household income, 20.8% of Henrico’s, and 19.2% of Chesterfield’s.
The ratio compares two medians, not one household’s rent and income: renters are on average lower-income than the all-household median, so a typical renter’s burden is higher than this ratio implies. The renter-income version below corrects for that, and the cost-burden section follows.









Figure 7






Annual median rent equals 34.2% of Richmond city’s median renter income, 31.0% of Henrico’s, and 31.4% of Chesterfield’s.
Rent and renter income are both renter-side medians, so this ratio is the closest single-number match to the cost-burden shares below (rent is gross rent; burden counts each household’s own income).







What these ratios do and don’t measure



Median home value is the owner’s own estimate of what their home is worth, for every owner-occupied home, not just recent sales, so the price-to-income ratio understates what it costs to enter the market today. The ratios appear twice, against all-household income and against renter-household income (ACS Table B25119); the renter version is the better yardstick for renters weighing a move to ownership. Both ratios divide one median by another; they describe how local prices compare with local incomes, not what any particular household can afford.

title: Market
section: Renter cost burden stayed near half while owner burden fell
text:
Renter cost burden stayed near half while owner burden fell








Figure 8






Across the region, 51.2% of renter households pay 30% or more of income on housing in the 2024 window, against 51.4% in the 2014 window — effectively unchanged. 25.7% pay half or more.
Owner burden fell: 20.0% of owners are cost-burdened now, down from 26.1%.
Richmond city has the highest owner burden of the core three (26.2%, down from 33.9%).
Renter burden is nearly identical across the core: 52.0% in Richmond city, 51.6% in Henrico, and 52.2% in Chesterfield — a region-wide condition, not a city one.
The Richmond MSA’s 51.2% renter burden compares with 48.5% statewide and 54.5% in Hampton Roads.

title: Market
section: Home-purchase lending peaked in 2021 and has settled lower
text:
Home-purchase lending peaked in 2021 and has settled lower








Figure 10






Across the core three, lenders originated 17,262 home-purchase loans for principal residences in 2021, the peak, and 10,607 in 2023, the low since (-38.6%). In 2025 it was 10,877.
Counting all purposes, originations were 49,661 in 2021, against 17,172 in 2023 and 20,984 in 2025; the swing is mostly refinancing, not buying.
In 2025, Chesterfield had 5,157 home-purchase originations, Henrico 3,729, and Richmond city 1,991.
Median originated loan in the core: $275,000 in 2018 and $365,000 in 2025 for home purchase (nominal dollars).









Figure 11






Over 2022-2025, 16.1% of Black applicants’ home-purchase applications were denied, against 4.5% for non-Hispanic White applicants, 10.6% for Hispanic or Latino applicants, and 9.0% for Asian applicants.
The overall home-purchase denial rate in the core was 8.3% in 2025 and 8.2% in 2018 — little changed. The all-purposes rate is higher (18.9% in 2025) because refinance and home-improvement applications are denied more often.
Denial rates by locality in 2025 are close: 7.5% in Richmond city, 8.4% in Henrico, and 8.6% in Chesterfield.

HMDA covers most mortgage lenders but not every loan, and the denial rate describes applications that reached a credit decision (originated, approved-but-not-accepted, or denied); withdrawn and incomplete applications are not counted. What eviction filings do and don’t measure



A filing is a landlord’s court request, not a completed eviction: many cases are dismissed, settled, or paid before judgment, and a household can be filed against more than once. Filings are a signal of housing instability, not a count of households displaced. The 2020-2021 collapse reflects pandemic-era eviction moratoria and rental assistance as much as underlying need, so read the recovery against the pre-2020 baseline, not as a measure of the renter burden shown above. Counts cover the three core localities only; the expansion ring is not included.








Small-geography reliability



Renter-burden and median estimates for the expansion-ring localities and other small jurisdictions rest on small samples. Figures here use the pooled rows or the three core localities where possible; locality-level cells with a coefficient of variation above 30 are omitted (—) and medium-reliability cells are marked (*).








How cost burden is measured



A household is cost-burdened when it pays 30% or more of its income on housing and severely cost-burdened at 50% or more. For renters, housing cost is gross rent, which includes utilities; for owners it is selected monthly owner costs, which include mortgage payments, taxes, insurance, and utilities. Households with no or negative income are excluded.








What this page shows




Tenure: about two-thirds of households own (67.0%), a share that barely moved, but Richmond city is a majority-renter locality (43.5% own).
Values and rents: the Richmond MSA’s median home value rose 24.1% and median rent rose 11.3% after inflation.
Affordability: the typical home was worth 4.1 times the typical household income in the metro (6.5 times the typical renter income), and median rent equalled 20.0% of household income (31.7% of renter income).
Cost burden: about half of renter households (51.2%) are cost-burdened and that has not eased, while owner burden fell to 20.0%.
Mortgage lending: core-three home-purchase originations for principal residences peaked at 17,262 in 2021 and were 10,877 in 2025; Black applicants were denied 16.1% of the time against 4.5% for White applicants.
Evictions: core-three filings fell 80% from the pre-2020 peak to the 2021 trough and now run at about 85% of the historical average.

section: The core is a single-family region; density is concentrated in the city
text:
The core is a single-family region; density is concentrated in the city








Figure 3






Single-family detached homes are 63.0% of the pooled core’s stock and 87.8% of the expansion ring’s.
Richmond city is the outlier: 21.6% of its units sit in buildings of 20 or more, against 7.2% in Henrico and 4.6% in Chesterfield.
Small multifamily (2–4 units) is scarce everywhere but the city, where it is 12.0% of stock versus 2.9% in Chesterfield and 0.9% in the expansion ring.
Manufactured housing is a rounding error in the core (0.7%) but 2.5% of the expansion ring and 12.6% of Ashland’s stock.







Small-geography reliability



Ashland is a town of roughly 3,164 housing units, so its ACS estimates carry wide margins of error — 2 of its 11 structure-type and year-built cells fall below the CV-30 reliability threshold. Ashland and the four expansion-ring localities are shown here only where the underlying estimate is reliable; suppressed cells appear as an em dash.

title: Inventory
section: Housing age splits the region in two
text:
Housing age splits the region in two








Figure 4






37.7% of Richmond city’s housing was built before 1950, against 7.4% in Henrico and 2.4% in Chesterfield.
Chesterfield’s stock is the region’s newest: 50.3% was built in 1990 or later, and 17.2% since 2010.
The expansion ring is newer still by that measure — 56.0% built since 1990 — consistent with its faster unit growth.
Only 13.2% of the pooled core’s stock dates from 2010 or later, so the great majority of the region’s housing predates the current market.

title: Inventory
section: Permitting recovered from the 2011 trough, and what gets permitted has changed
text:
Permitting recovered from the 2011 trough, and what gets permitted has changed








Figure 5






Regional permitting peaked at 10,414 units in 2022 and bottomed at 2,520 in 2011 — a 76% collapse.
The 2025 total of 9,091 units is still below the 2022 peak, but roughly 3.6 times the trough.
Multifamily was 3.6% of permitted units in 2000 and 51.6% in 2025; it first exceeded single-family in 2022.
Single-family permitting has been flat at roughly 4,400–5,900 units a year since 2020, so essentially all of the swing in regional volume is multifamily.

Over the last five years the core three localities accounted for 37,448 of the region’s 47,667 permitted units — 79% of regional production.
Richmond city permitted 9,126 multifamily units in five years, more than Henrico (7,549) and Chesterfield (5,857), despite being the smallest of the three by stock.
Chesterfield is the region’s single-family engine, with 8,902 single-family permits — more than double Henrico’s.
The expansion ring permitted 6,719 single-family units against only 371 multifamily, a 5.2% multifamily share.









Figure 6






Richmond city’s multifamily share rose from 50.7% in 2015 to 86.3% in 2025 — the city now permits almost nothing but apartments.
Chesterfield peaked at 57.2% multifamily in 2022 and fell back to 28.2% by 2025, returning to a single-family pattern.
Henrico is the most volatile of the three, swinging between 24.5% (2016) and 73.4% (2023).
The three localities diverged after 2021: before then their multifamily shares moved roughly together, and since then they have not.







What this page establishes



The Richmond region’s existing stock is overwhelmingly single-family and largely predates 1990, with density and prewar housing both concentrated in Richmond city. New production tells a different story — since 2022 the region has permitted more multifamily than single-family units, driven almost entirely by the city and Henrico, while the expansion ring continues to build detached houses almost exclusively. Vacancy is low across the core and the ring, so the stock that exists is being used; the region’s slack sits in its southern localities. The Demographics and Market pages cover who lives in this housing and what it costs.

title: Chesterfield One-Pager Implementation Plan
text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: Build chesterfield-onepager.qmd, a one-page BHC-branded page that renders to HTML and to a single-page PDF, showing what Chesterfield public-service workers earn and what one income affords in rent and home price.
Architecture: One script curates the sourced pay rows and validates them (r/chesterfield_pay.R); a second turns pay into affordability figures against Chesterfield’s ACS median rent and home value (r/chesterfield_afford.R); the page reads only the resulting .rds and renders with the typst and html formats. Pages never call APIs.
Tech Stack: R (tidyverse, ggplot2, ggtext, kableExtra), Quarto 1.6.39 (Typst PDF), _common.R, _brand.yml.
Spec: design/2026-11-23-chesterfield-one-pager-design.md



Follow CLAUDE.md script anatomy: header comment (what, source, output), numbered ## 1. Setup ---- sections, .Renviron fallback if a key is needed, write_rds() paired with export_csv(), a validation block. Scripts are idempotent.
Pages call read_rds() only. No salaries typed into the .qmd.
Native pipe |>, tidyverse style, janitor::clean_names() on imported raw data.
Narrative rule: takeaway H2s/title, 2-5 bullets, callouts for caveats. No drafted paragraphs.
Charts: theme_rva(), palette from _common.R only (rva_pal, rva_seq, rva_brand), #| fig-alt: on every figure, currency via scales::label_dollar(), title is a takeaway sentence, subtitle carries geography, units and years, caption from a _common.R helper.
Single-earner headline. Maximum affordable rent is 30% of gross monthly income. Hourly pay is annualized at 2,080 hours and labeled as such.
Every pay row carries source, source_date and status (current, proposed, or stale). A proposed or stale figure is never labeled “current” on the page.
Commit types: data(...), content(...), docs(...). End commits with Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>.
R and Quarto may not be on PATH; see README.md for the prepend. User runs any job over about two minutes. Paths are relative to the project root with forward slashes.





A figure marked proposed or stale must not appear on the page as “current” (the callout and table must show its status).
A pay row with a missing source, source_date, or status fails validation instead of rendering.
Hourly roles show the 2,080-hour annualization and a school-year caveat, so a full-time figure is not presented as actual earnings.
The PDF is exactly one page; a longer table or caption must not spill onto a second page.
Rent and home figures come from the 2020-2024 ACS window while pay is 2026: the caption states both vintages.




Files: - Create: r/chesterfield_pay.R - Output: data/chesterfield_pay.rds, data-out/chesterfield_pay.csv
Interfaces: - Produces: tibble pay with columns role (chr), employer (chr: “County” or “CCPS”), basis (chr: “annual” or “hourly”), amount (dbl, as published), annual_pay (dbl; hourly x 2080 rounded to whole dollars), source (chr), source_date (Date), status (chr: “current”, “proposed”, “stale”), note (chr).

Step 1: Resolve the adoption check. Look up the adopted FY27 CCPS budget (School Board and Board of Supervisors) for teacher step 0, instructional assistant step 0, and bus driver T1 step 1. Re-check the Deputy Sheriff starting pay on the current county posting. If a figure is confirmed adopted or posted for FY27, set status = "current" and cite the adopted document; otherwise leave proposed/stale. Record what you found in the note column.
Step 2: Write the validation block first at the bottom of the script, asserting: 7 roles present (teacher, instructional assistant, school bus driver, police officer, firefighter/EMT, deputy sheriff, 911 officer); no NA in role, annual_pay, source, source_date, status; status %in% c("current","proposed","stale"); every hourly row has annual_pay == round(amount * 2080); police annual_pay == 60147, firefighter/EMT annual_pay == 60147, 911 officer annual_pay == 48447, teacher (FY26) annual_pay == 55047. Run it with the curated tibble stubbed empty and confirm it fails.
Step 2b: Run to see it fail. Run: Rscript r/chesterfield_pay.R. Expected: stopifnot error naming the missing roles.
Step 3: Fill the curated tribble() in the script (one row per role, values from the design doc’s pay table plus Step 1 results; teacher gets both the FY26 current row and, unless adopted, an FY27 proposed row). Compute annual_pay, write with write_rds() and export_csv(pay, "chesterfield_pay").
Step 4: Run to see it pass. Run: Rscript r/chesterfield_pay.R. Expected: no error; data/chesterfield_pay.rds and data-out/chesterfield_pay.csv exist.
Step 5: Commit. data(chesterfield-pay): add curated public-service starting pay with sources.




Files: - Create: r/chesterfield_afford.R - Output: data/chesterfield_onepager.rds, data-out/chesterfield_onepager.csv
Interfaces: - Consumes: data/chesterfield_pay.rds (Task 1 pay); data/acs_market.rds rows with geoid == "51041", year == 2024, measure %in% c("median_rent", "median_value"), column estimate; data/summary_county_5176099999.csv (HUD FY2026 limits, 80% AMI one-person limit $63,600). - Produces: afford tibble: all columns of pay plus max_rent (dbl, annual_pay * 0.30 / 12), max_price (dbl), rent_gap (dbl, max_rent - median_rent), price_gap (dbl, max_price - median_value), pct_ami80_1p (dbl, annual_pay / 63600); and a list ctx with median_rent, median_value, assumptions (one-row tibble: rate, rate_source, rate_date, down_pct, tax_rate, tax_source, ins_rate, pmi_rate). Saved together as a named list list(afford = , ctx = ) in the .rds.

Step 1: Write the validation block first: max_rent for $60,147 equals 1503.675 (within 0.01); round-trip check, i.e. for every row the monthly PITI at max_price equals annual_pay * 0.30 / 12 within $1; Chesterfield median_rent == 1629 and median_value == 366000 (same-vintage ACS figures already in data/acs_market.rds); assumptions has non-empty rate_source, rate_date, tax_source. Run: Rscript r/chesterfield_afford.R. Expected: fails (no data yet).
Step 2: Implement max_price(income, rate, down_pct, tax_rate, ins_rate, pmi_rate) -> dbl in the script. Algorithm: budget B = income * 0.30 / 12; monthly mortgage factor m = r/12 / (1 - (1 + r/12)^-360); price = B / ((1 - down_pct) * m + tax_rate/12 + ins_rate/12 + (1 - down_pct) * pmi_rate/12), with pmi_rate forced to 0 when down_pct >= 0.20.
Step 3: Source the assumptions and enter them in the assumptions tibble: the latest Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year rate (record the date), Chesterfield’s current real-estate tax rate per $100 from chesterfield.gov (record the URL), a stated down payment, homeowners insurance rate and PMI rate. Write each source into the tibble. Join pay to the ACS and HUD values, compute the columns above, write_rds() and export_csv().
Step 4: Run. Rscript r/chesterfield_afford.R. Expected: validation passes; log the rent and price gaps per role in LOG.md later.
Step 5: Commit. data(chesterfield-afford): compute affordable rent and price by role.




Files: - Create: chesterfield-onepager.qmd - Modify: _common.R (add caption helper chesterfield_pay_cap() -> chr)
Interfaces: - Consumes: data/chesterfield_onepager.rds list afford and ctx from Task 2. - Produces: docs/chesterfield-onepager.html and docs/chesterfield-onepager.pdf (one page).

Step 1: Add chesterfield_pay_cap(...) to _common.R: bold-markdown “Source:” line naming Chesterfield County HR postings, Chesterfield County Public Schools’ Feb 3, 2026 compensation presentation, the 2020-2024 ACS 5-year (Tables B25064, B25077), and HUD FY2026 income limits.
Step 2: Write the QMD front matter: title is a takeaway sentence; format: with html (site theme, links to the PDF at chesterfield-onepager.pdf) and typst (letter paper, narrow margins, _brand.yml brand, horizontal logo in the header, toc: false). If Typst does not apply the brand fonts or logo acceptably, fall back to pdf with latex-engine: xelatex, and note it in LOG.md.
Step 3: Setup chunk (source("_common.R"), read_rds("data/chesterfield_onepager.rds"), inline scalars for the big numbers). Body in this order: three big-number callouts (median rent, teacher max rent, police/fire max rent); chart fig-pay-vs-afford (starting pay by role as bars, with lines for the pay needed to afford the median rent and the median home, bold ggtext subtitle spans, no legend); table tbl-roles (role, starting pay, status, max rent, max home price, vs. median rent) via kbl() |> kable_styling(c("condensed","striped")) and a dual-income line; 2-5 bullets; a caveat callout (proposed vs adopted via status, 2,080-hour annualization, school-year schedules, 2020-2024 ACS vs 2026 pay); a sources footer from chesterfield_pay_cap().
Step 4: Render HTML. Run: quarto render chesterfield-onepager.qmd --to html. Expected: no error, fig-pay-vs-afford has fig-alt.
Step 5: Render the PDF and confirm one page. Run: quarto render chesterfield-onepager.qmd --to typst, then pdftotext docs/chesterfield-onepager.pdf - and count form-feed characters. Expected: exactly 1 page. If it overflows, shrink the table and chart, not the caveat callout.
Step 6: Eyeball the PDF (open docs/chesterfield-onepager.pdf): logo, brand colors, legible table, no clipped text.
Step 7: Commit. content(chesterfield-onepager): add one-page Chesterfield affordability brief.

Step 1: Add the navbar entry and a data-notes.qmd paragraph covering sources, dates, status meaning, the 30%-of-income rule, and the home-price assumptions with their sources.
Step 2: Update CLAUDE.md repo map, and TODO.md: check off this work, add the open items (adopted FY27 confirmation if not resolved, BHC logo clearance, firefighter/sheriff pay-plan step tables).
Step 3: Append a LOG.md entry: what was built, the data surprises (the class-spec police minimum of $53,214 predates FY24 raises; the CCPS deck’s $57,227 vs $57,277 typo; Deputy Sheriff pay from a January posting), and what is left open.

Step 5: Commit. docs: wire Chesterfield one-pager into site, update TODO and LOG.

title: Demographics
section: The region has outgrown Virginia in nearly every year since 2011
text:
The region has outgrown Virginia in nearly every year since 2011








Figure 2






Between 2011 and 2025 the 17-locality region grew faster than Virginia in 13 of 14 years.
The region’s fastest year was 2024, when it grew 1.47% (19,910 people).
Virginia’s growth slowed to 0.24% at its low point; the region never dropped below 0.74%.
Population Estimates Program figures and the ACS windows above measure different periods and use different methods, so their growth rates are not interchangeable.

text:
Migration, not births, now drives the region’s growth

Natural increase (births minus deaths) fell from 4,228 people a year in 2010-2019 to 1,451 a year in 2020-2025.
Net migration rose: 7,298 a year in 2010-2019 and 13,035 a year in 2020-2025, so it supplied 63% of growth in the first era and 90% in the second.
International migration peaked in 2024 at 10,787 people, well above any earlier year; domestic migration stayed between 6,069 and 7,543 a year after 2020.
In 10 of the 17 localities, deaths exceeded births over 2020-2025.

title: Demographics
section: Richmond city turned from domestic to international growth
text:
Richmond city turned from domestic to international growth








Figure 4






Richmond city’s international migration rate rose from 2.8 to 6.8 per 1,000 residents a year, while its domestic rate swung from +5.3 to -1.1.
Henrico lost residents to domestic migration in both eras (-0.5 and -3.1) and grew on international migration (7.0 in 2020-2025).
Chesterfield’s growth is mostly domestic movers: 10.0 domestic against 4.2 international per 1,000 in 2020-2025.
The expansion ring’s net rate of 18.8 per 1,000 a year is almost entirely domestic (17.9).









Figure 5






Net migration rates rose in 14 of the 17 localities between 2010-2019 and 2020-2025; the highest in 2020-2025 were New Kent (36.6 per 1,000 a year) and Goochland (35.2).
The region’s rate rose from 5.9 to 9.7 per 1,000, against 2.4 to 4.1 for Virginia.
The 3 localities whose rate was no higher in the 2020s than in the 2010s are Henrico, Prince George, and Richmond city.







How to read the migration estimates



Population Estimates Program migration figures are modeled from administrative records, not counted, and are revised each vintage. Net migration is international plus domestic; domestic migration is the net balance of moves between this locality and the rest of the United States. The 2010-2019 and 2020-2025 series come from different vintages, the second built on the 2020 Census, so the page compares the eras instead of joining them. The 2010 and 2020 components cover only April to June and are omitted, and a small residual (not shown) accounts for the rest of each year’s change.

title: Demographics
section: The region is aging, and the expansion ring is aging fastest
text:
The region is aging, and the expansion ring is aging fastest








Figure 6






The region’s 65-and-over share rose from 12.9% to 16.7%, while its under-18 share fell from 22.7% to 21.3%.
The expansion ring is the oldest geography: 20.0% are 65 or over, up +5.4 points since the 2014 window.
Richmond city is the youngest of the three core localities at 14.1% 65 and over, and has the smallest share of children of the three (17.5%).
Chesterfield has the largest share of children among the core three (23.7%), though that share also fell over the decade.

title: Demographics
section: Diversity grew across the region, but Richmond city moved the other way
text:
Diversity grew across the region, but Richmond city moved the other way








Figure 7






The region’s White non-Hispanic share fell from 58.7% to 54.7%; the Hispanic or Latino share rose from 5.5% to 8.4%.
Richmond city went the other direction: its White non-Hispanic share rose from 39.7% to 41.4%, and its Black share fell from 48.6% to 40.6%.
Chesterfield and Henrico diversified: their White non-Hispanic shares fell to 56.4% and 49.5%, and Henrico’s Asian share reached 9.4%.
The expansion ring remains the least diverse geography, at 80.3% White non-Hispanic.







Read the multiracial change with care



The “Multiracial” share roughly doubled in the region, but part of that is measurement, not demographic change. The Census Bureau revised how it codes and processes write-in race responses beginning with 2020 data, which raised the count of people classified as two or more races. The 2014 window predates that change and the 2024 window includes it, so treat the multiracial trend as partly methodological.

title: Demographics
section: Household makeup splits the same way: singles in the city, married couples in the ring
text:
Household makeup splits the same way: singles in the city, married couples in the ring








Figure 8






People living alone are 43.1% of Richmond city households, against 30.6% in Henrico, 22.9% in Chesterfield, and 21.1% in the expansion ring.
Married-couple families are 61.4% of expansion-ring households and 54.8% of Chesterfield’s, but only 24.6% of Richmond city’s.
Across the whole region, 29.6% of households are one person — a household type that often fits a smaller unit than the detached single-family homes that dominate the stock (see the Inventory page).

title: Demographics
section: Typical renters earn well under the typical household in every geography
text:
Typical renters earn well under the typical household in every geography








Figure 10






The Richmond MSA’s median renter household income was $54,728 in 2024 dollars, 63.1% of the all-household median ($86,679). It rose 14.1% in real terms, against 9.6% for all households.
Among the core three, renter income is 74.6% of the all-household median in Richmond city, 67.1% in Henrico, and 61.1% in Chesterfield. Richmond city’s real renter income rose 25.5%, Henrico’s 10.7%, and Chesterfield’s 5.5%.
This is the income the Market page and the summary set against home values and rents, because renters are the group that would be moving toward ownership.









Figure 11






20.2% of Richmond city households earn under $25,000, against 8.4% in Chesterfield and 7.6% in the expansion ring.
At the top, 34.4% of expansion-ring households earn $150,000 or more, against 29.2% in Chesterfield and 18.1% in Richmond city.
Income bands are fixed nominal thresholds, so a rising share in the top band partly reflects inflation, not only real gains.

title: Demographics
section: Renter households skew far lower-income than owners
text:
Renter households skew far lower-income than owners








Figure 12






Across the region, 45.9% of renter households earn under $50,000, against 18.9% of owner households.
In Richmond city, 51.9% of renters and 24.0% of owners fall under that line.
Even in the expansion ring, where incomes are highest, 36.1% of renters earn under $50,000 — the rental market there serves a lower-income group than the ownership market does.







Small-geography reliability



Ashland and the four expansion-ring localities have much smaller samples than the core. 5 of the 30 race-and-ethnicity cells for those five geographies fall below the CV-30 reliability threshold in the 2024 window. Figures here use the pooled expansion-ring row, and tables suppress low-reliability cells (—) and mark medium-reliability ones (*).








What this page shows




Growth: the region grew 10.7%, led by Chesterfield and the expansion ring, and outgrew Virginia in 13 of 14 years.
Migration: net migration supplied 90% of regional growth in 2020-2025, as natural increase fell.
Age: the 65-and-over share rose in every geography, and the expansion ring is the oldest.
Race and ethnicity: the region diversified, but Richmond city’s White share rose while its Black share fell.
Households: living alone dominates in Richmond city (43.1%); married couples dominate in the ring.
Income: real median income rose everywhere, and renters earn far less than owners (median renter income is 63.1% of the metro’s all-household median) — the gap the market page turns into cost burden.

title: CLAUDE.md — RVA SOURCEBOOK
text:
Conventions for all Claude sessions on this project. This is a personal/portfolio Quarto website, not a client deliverable — a public sourcebook of basic Richmond-region housing data (inventory, demographics, market) built from public sources only. TODO.md is the punch list — start every session there. METHODOLOGY.md holds the internal data/geography/scope conventions; data-notes.qmd holds the public-facing methodology. PLAN.md has the target architecture and phased build order.



Read this file, then TODO.md, then the top entry of LOG.md.
Read METHODOLOGY.md and _common.R for the geography/scope rules that bear on the task at hand.
Verify that any prerequisite raw files exist under data/raw/ (there aren’t many — this project runs almost entirely on API pulls). If any are missing, do the work that doesn’t need them and record the blocker in the log entry.





Update TODO.md — check off what landed, add anything new that surfaced.
Append a LOG.md entry: what changed, data surprises, what was left open.
Update README.md or this file if a convention changed — same session, not a follow-up.
Commit the work and the log entry together.







Setting
Value




Repo type
Report / personal site


Commit types
fix, docs, chore, data, content, infra


Scope
A component noun (docs(readme), data(acs-tenure), content(market)). Optional on docs and chore commits.


Versioned
No. Git history plus LOG.md is the release record







Start narrow. Read TODO.md and only the LOG.md/METHODOLOGY.md sections that bear on the task. Do not read whole files when a block will do.
Model guidance. Sonnet is fine for mechanical data pulls, geography swaps, and QA sweeps, as well as page/chart builds — this project doesn’t carry the methodology weight that would call for Opus by default.
User runs long jobs — tigris pulls, renv package installs, and any full render over roughly two minutes. Claude writes the script; user runs it and pastes back errors and validation output. Never babysit a long Rscript run.
Skills carry the boilerplate. Invoke /new-data-script before writing a new r/*.R pull or prep script — it lives in-repo at .claude/new-data-script/. It reads the project-config block from this file, METHODOLOGY.md, and _common.R at invocation.




r/ scripts write data/*.rds and, through export_csv(), data-out/*.csv. Pages call read_rds() only. Pages never call APIs.



Script anatomy: a header comment stating what, source, and output → numbered ## 1. Setup ---- sections → an .Renviron fallback for keys → write_rds() paired with export_csv() → a validation block. Scripts are idempotent and safe to re-run. No inline install.packages().

Native pipe |>, tidyverse style, janitor::clean_names() on all imported raw data.
dplyr 1.2 idioms once pinned via renv: .by= over group_by() for one-off grouping; across(); join_by(); reframe() for multi-row summaries. Prefer recode_values()/case_match() for value-to-label recodes over nested case_when(); reserve case_when() for genuine conditional logic.
purrr::map() and imap() over for loops, bound with list_rbind()/list_cbind() (or map_dfr()/map_dfc() if the pinned purrr predates 1.2). Pattern: map(years, \(yr) get_acs(..., year = yr) |> mutate(year = yr)) |> list_rbind().
tidycensus: get_acs(geography, state = "VA", table = "BXXXXX", year, survey = "acs5", cache_table = TRUE). Pull whole tables and build label lookups from load_variables() with separate_wider_delim(label, "!!").





stopifnot() fires only on structural expectations (row counts, all geographies present, no all-NA columns) and on same-vintage published benchmarks — a Census-published table total or another public, dated figure.
Vintage-to-vintage comparisons (e.g. an older ACS window vs. the current one) are a logged percentage change in the session’s log entry, never a stopifnot() gate — different 5-year windows differ by construction, and an implausible swing is a flag for review, not a build failure.
Every data script logs its benchmark results, both passes and variances.





Geography: rr (17-locality Richmond region), bhc (3-locality core: Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield), secondary (4 expansion localities: Hanover, Goochland, New Kent, Powhatan), ashland (place 5103368, sumlev 160), regions (comparison MSAs: Charlottesville, Richmond, Hampton Roads, DC), virginia; and PUMA sets puma_core3/puma_region/puma_locality, used by r/pums/ and profiles.qmd (profiles.qmd covers the core three only, via puma_core3 — see METHODOLOGY.md).
Palette/theme: rva_pal (8-hue categorical, fixed order — never cycle or reorder), rva_seq (7-step blue sequential ramp for choropleths/magnitude), rva_ink (chart chrome: primary/muted/gridline/baseline), rva_brand (Better Housing Coalition brand colors; mirrors _brand.yml, which drives site and deck fonts, colors, and logo — change both together), theme_rva() (ggplot2 theme; legend.position = "none" by default since 2-3 series use bold ggtext subtitle spans instead of a legend box), and rva_map_style (free Carto MapLibre basemap URL, no token). Values come from the dataviz skill’s validated reference palette — CVD-safe adjacent pairs. Change values in _common.R only, never at the call site.
Caption helpers: acs_cap, pums_cap, chas_cap, dec_cap, pep_cap, bps_cap, oews_cap and others — see the file for the full list. Not every helper has a matching script yet; that’s fine, they’re cheap to keep around.
flag_reliability(df, cv_col = cv) — High at or below 15, Medium at or below 30, Low above 30, from a 0 to 100 CV. Use it for secondary-locality and Ashland ACS estimates, which run noisier than the bhc core.
export_csv(df, name) — writes data-out/<name>.csv. All data in this project is public-source, so no filename-prefix privacy convention is needed (unlike sibling reports that mix in licensed MLS/CoStar data).
fct_wrap(f, width) — applies str_wrap() to a factor’s levels.





Titles are takeaway sentences. The subtitle carries geography, units, and years. Captions come from a _common.R source helper.
For 2 or 3 series, prefer color-coded bold words in the subtitle (ggtext spans) over a legend.
Keep subtitle length to roughly 50 characters to avoid wrapping onto a new row.
Currency uses scales::label_dollar(), and the subtitle notes whether a series is nominal or inflation-adjusted. Percentages use label_percent(accuracy = 1) unless precision matters.
Tables use kbl() |> kable_styling(c("condensed","striped")) with formattable::comma and percent.
Secondary-locality and Ashland ACS estimates always carry reliability treatment through flag_reliability(). Suppress cells with a CV above 30 and footnote the Medium cells.
Every figure gets #| fig-alt: alt text.





Use mapgl for anything inherently spatial (locality choropleths, point maps of permits/listings); keep everything else as static ggplot2.
Basemap: rva_map_style in _common.R — Carto’s free Positron MapLibre style, no Mapbox token, zero-cost. Revisit only if styling needs genuinely outgrow that.
Choropleth fills use rva_seq (the same sequential ramp as ggplot2 magnitude encodings), so a reader sees one consistent “light = low, dark = high” language across static charts and maps.
Boundary data comes from r/geo.R → data/geo.rds (tigris pulls for the rr region). Join whatever table a map needs onto that, in the page — don’t re-pull boundaries per page.
Caption maps the same way as charts, via a _common.R source helper.




Pages ship with takeaway H2s, 2 to 5 bullet findings per section (plain statements traceable to a figure or table), and callout boxes for data caveats. No drafted paragraphs. The bullets should be specific enough that they could be expanded into prose without reopening the data, even though this is a personal project and that expansion may never happen.



Never run R inline. Write r/<name>.R and run Rscript r/<name>.R from the project root. Ad hoc checks go in a temp script in the scratchpad, run through Rscript, never in the repo.
R and Quarto are usually not on PATH. See README.md for the prepend and render commands once it’s written; install paths are machine-specific.
Use forward slashes in R paths, and keep every path relative to the project root.



CENSUS_API_KEY is required for tidycensus. It lives in the user .Renviron at %USERPROFILE%\Documents\.Renviron. Never print or commit its value. A FRED_API_KEY may be added later if CPI/PMMS series get pulled in.
R’s HOME on Windows may be C:\Users\<you> rather than the Documents folder, so that file is not always loaded automatically. Scripts include an .Renviron fallback derived from the current user — readRenviron(file.path(Sys.getenv("USERPROFILE"), "Documents", ".Renviron")) when the key is empty — never a hardcoded username. Verify visibility with a TRUE or FALSE check only.



tidycensus, tigris, and (if added) fredr package downloads are approved. Direct fetches from census.gov file servers (e.g. BPS permit text files) are approved with a manual fallback. Anything else on a government host, especially BLS OEWS/QCEW beyond what a package wraps, gets a quick sanity check before scripting — this is a solo project, so “approval” just means pausing to confirm the source and terms of use look right before pulling.



Not yet published. Intended as a public GitHub Pages site (docs/ on main) once the first three pages (inventory, demographics, market) have real content. No review workflow, no annotation tooling — it’s a personal project.




dplyr::join_by(a == b) on differently-named columns — the joined result keeps only a, silently dropping b. A downstream mutate()/select() expecting b gets a column-not-found error, or an NA after a bind_rows() masks the missing column with a same-named one from another frame. Join on equal-named keys only and enforce cross-name equality with a filter() immediately after, so both columns survive.
PEP — the post-2020 API requires an explicit vintage= argument; year= alone misbehaves silently. Fall back to the FTP tables if the API lags.

(This section previously carried several PUMS/CHAS/MLS-specific gotchas inherited from a sibling project’s CLAUDE.md. They referenced scripts that don’t exist in this repo and were removed on 2026-09-15. If PUMS or CHAS work ever starts here, re-derive gotchas from this project’s own scripts rather than reusing the old list.)

section: Seniors and smaller households need smaller homes
text:
Seniors and smaller households need smaller homes
















How to read these figures



One earner, starting pay. Affordable rent is 30% of gross income; cost burden means 30% or more of income goes to housing. Home price assumes a 7.11% 30-year mortgage (Freddie Mac, week of Nov 12, 2026), 5% down, the county’s proposed FY2027 real estate tax rate ($0.89 per $100), insurance at 0.35% of price and mortgage insurance at 0.7% of the loan (the last two are our assumptions). Hourly pay is annualized at 2,080 hours; school-year workers earn less. Teacher and bus driver pay is the FY26 scale; FY27 pay is proposed, not confirmed adopted. Deputy sheriff pay is from a January 2026 posting; the 911 officer figure is the class-specification minimum. AMI is HUD’s FY2026 area median income for the Richmond area, adjusted for household size. Median rent and home value are 2020-2024 ACS.


Sources: Chesterfield County HR postings and class specifications (retrieved Nov 23, 2026); Chesterfield County Public Schools, compensation presentation, Feb 3, 2026; U.S. Census Bureau, 2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates, Tables B25064, B25077, B25070, B25091, B25072, B25093, B25009, B25042, B25007, B01001 and B11001; ACS 2020-2024 PUMS household incomes against HUD FY2026 income limits (Richmond HUD Metro FMR Area), adjusted for household size; Census Population Estimates Program, Vintages 2019 and 2025.

Chesterfield one-pager: pay and affordability
The Chesterfield one-pager uses starting pay from the county’s own postings and class specifications and from Chesterfield County Public Schools’ February 3, 2026 compensation presentation, all retrieved November 23, 2026. Each pay figure carries its source, date and a status: current (latest figure confirmed in the source), proposed (not confirmed adopted) or stale (predates the current fiscal year). title: RVA Sourcebook
text:
A basic reference for Richmond-region housing data — inventory, demographics, and market conditions — pulled from public sources (Census/ACS, BLS) and kept current as new data releases.

Inventory — housing stock, occupancy, structure type, permits
Demographics — population, households, income
Market — tenure, home values, rents, cost burden

See Data Notes for sources and methodology, and About for what this project is.

Data surprises:

What changed: Added r/pep_migration.R (user request): PEP births, deaths, natural change, international and domestic migration for the 17 rr localities, pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17, and Virginia. Source is the Census co-est2019-alldata.csv (2010–2019) and co-est2025-alldata.csv (2020–2025) files, cached under data/cache/pep/. Outputs data/pep_migration.rds (annual + era frames) and two CSVs. Added three H2 sections to demographics.qmd after the population-growth section (4 figures, 1 table, a callout), plus a migration bullet in the closing summary. Documented the vintage and partial-year rules in METHODOLOGY.md.
Design decisions: The files are used instead of tidycensus::get_estimates() because the API returns only a vintage’s latest year (probed: vintage 2025 → year 2025 only), so a series from it would mix revised and unrevised vintages. The two vintages don’t join — the 2019 → 2020 regional step (1,291,900 → 1,316,683) spans the 2020 Census rebase — so annual change is never computed across it and the page compares eras. The 2010 and 2020 components are April–June only (Richmond city births: 765 in 2020 vs. 2,872 in 2021) and are NA. Ran the script myself (two cached CSVs plus one tiny API call, ~7 s) since it isn’t a long pull.
Data surprises:

Natural increase collapsed; migration didn’t. Region: natural change 38,050 over 2011–2019 (4,228/yr) vs. 7,254 over 2021–2025 (1,451/yr); net migration 65,684 (7,298/yr) vs. 65,176 (13,035/yr). Migration share of growth 63% → 90%. 10 of 17 localities had more deaths than births in 2020–2025.
Region outgrew Virginia in 13 of 14 years (all but 2011). 2024 was the peak at +1.47% (19,910 people), driven by a record 10,787 international migrants.
Richmond city flipped. Domestic net migration +5.3 → −1.1 per 1,000/yr; international 2.8 → 6.8. Henrico’s domestic is negative in both eras (−0.5, −3.1). Chesterfield and the expansion ring are domestic-driven; the ring’s net rate is 18.8/1,000/yr with negative natural change (migration share 106%).
14 of 17 localities had a higher net migration rate in the 2020s; Henrico, Prince George, and Richmond city did not. New Kent (36.6) and Goochland (35.2) lead.
Validation: all component identities hold exactly in both files (Δpop = natural + net migration + residual; net = international + domestic); rr17 reconciles to its 17 members in all 16 years; 2025 population and net migration match the Census API (Vintage 2025) for all 17 localities.
Bugs caught: p_fmt(x, 0) — its second argument is accuracy, not digits — rendered a title as “Migration supplied NA of growth” (fixed to 1); formattable::percent() can’t mix with a character in if_else(). The shell also choked on a long heredoc, so the page patch ran from a script file.

Data surprises:

B25036 is not published in the 2014 window. The TODO line asked for B25034–36; including B25036 would have broken the three-window trend every other frame carries, so it is out of scope for v1 and recorded as such in METHODOLOGY.md. B25035 is a median and cannot be summed, so it is pulled but carries no pooled rows.
BPS file naming is a trap. co<YY><MM>y.txt is year-to-date-through-month and ...c.txt is the monthly current file; only co<YYYY>a.txt is the true annual file. Confirmed the layout against both the 2000 and 2025 files before writing the parser. The files also carry each size class twice — a published imputation-inclusive figure and a “rep” reported-only duplicate. This script reads the former.
Both cross-table checks reconciled exactly. B25024 and B25034 each sum to B25001 at 0.000% max difference across every geography-year, and B25002’s Occupied + Vacant equals its own Total everywhere. Tighter than the 0.5% tolerance allowed for.
The regional permit story is compositional, not volumetric. Permitted units ran 6,110 (2000) → 8,912 (2002) → a 2,520 trough in 2011 → a 10,414 peak in 2022 → 9,091 in 2025. Multifamily went from 3.6% of permitted units in 2000 to 56.8% in 2022, first exceeding single-family that year. Richmond city is now at 86.3% multifamily while Chesterfield fell back to 28.2% — the three core localities diverged sharply after 2021.
Housing-unit growth, 2014 → 2024 (logged, not gated): Richmond core +13.3% (357,302 → 404,918), Chesterfield +17.1%, Richmond city +15.3%, Henrico +8.3%, expansion ring +18.4%, Ashland +14.3%.

Switched plot.caption to element_textbox_simple() with width = unit(1, "npc"). Found by reading the rendered PNGs; the render exit code was clean throughout.
formattable masks scales. _common.R loads formattable after scales, so comma()/percent() resolve to formattable’s, which take digits rather than accuracy — this killed two renders outright and silently produced “357,302.00” unit counts in a table. inventory.qmd uses local n_fmt()/p_fmt() wrappers for inline prose and passes digits = 0 to the kbl() cells.
12 of 30 Ashland structure-type and year-built cells fall below CV-30. The page computes that count rather than hardcoding it, and suppresses Low cells while marking Medium ones.

What changed: Fixed the senior-count sample size. The pages said “about 50 sample households” (hardcoded) and the audit said “roughly 115” (n_obs x share, which double-counts the share). In a PUMS profile row n_obs is already the unweighted record count in the category, so the true figure is 509 records (226 + 283) for core-three renters at or below 50% of AMI with a householder 65+, and 910 for owners. r/summary_audit.R now sums n_obs (sen_n()); summary.qmd and presentation.qmd compute senior_renters_n instead of typing a number. The audit’s renter_gt120_b30 note reported the smaller category (10 cases); it now reports 42 sample cases of 1,081 renter households above 120% of AMI.

text:
What changed: Added summary.qmd (executive summary: at-a-glance table, one section per page, “what to watch” box; every number computed from the page .rds files). Then, at the user’s request, a PUMS profile pipeline and page: r/pums/pums_profiles.R → data/pums_profiles.rds (+ two CSVs), profiles.qmd (households and residents by AMI band; each band profiled by owner/renter: household type, size, householder age and race, earners, disability, structure, cost burden, resident age/education/employment, medians), a “Lower-income renters carry the cost burden” section and sixth watch item in summary.qmd, and navbar entries for both pages. Updated METHODOLOGY.md (PUMS is now in use) and CLAUDE.md (PUMA sets, repo map).
Design decisions: The user’s r/pums/ scripts left no profile-ready dataset — pums_prep.R writes to data-in/pums/ and needs lookups that don’t exist — so pums_profiles.R builds from pums_raw/pums_wgt/rva_ami_pums directly. Profiles use five bands (≤30, 31–50, 51–80, 81–120, >120% AMI; zero/negative income folded into the first) because 8 bands × 2 tenures leave thin cells; the 8-band distribution is kept in ami_dist. SEs use the 80 replicate weights, computed in the script so the page never touches them. Vacant/group-quarters rows (TEN == "b", 2,516) are excluded — their income is missing and would otherwise land in “121%+”.
Data surprises:

Geography is not rr. The nine PUMAs cover 465,726 households / 1,140,000 residents; southern localities are out and two PUMAs mix localities. Called out at the top of the page and in the summary. Benchmark vs. ACS B25003 for the core-3 PUMAs (same 2020–2024 window): owners +0.35%, renters −0.59%.
38.4% of households are at or below 80% AMI — 59.8% of renters, 28.2% of owners. Richmond city is 50.9%, but only 41.7% of the region’s ≤80% AMI renter households live there.
Burden is steep and tenure-split: 80.3% of ≤30% AMI renters pay half or more of income on housing (owners: 64.4%); the renter–owner gap in 30%+ burden is widest at 31–50% AMI (87.0% vs 54.7%) and closes by 81–120% (16.9% vs 15.2%).
Reliability: counts and medians are all High; of 460 band × tenure shares, 50 are Medium and 9 Low, all small categories (<9.8% of a band; Low <2.5%).
Inventory page error found: its “peak … 76% collapse” line treats 2022’s 10,414 (the series high) as the pre-crash peak (~8,400 in 2005). Not fixed (out of scope); logged in TODO. The summary words permits as “bottomed in 2011, series high in 2022”.
Bugs caught before they shipped: I had written several alt-text and bullet claims ahead of the numbers and checked them afterward; seven were wrong (e.g. “57% of owners above 120% AMI” is 51.6%; “renters outnumber owners at 51–80%” is 42.6%; “White largest group in every band” fails for the two lowest renter bands; Hispanic renter share peaks at 31–50%, not 51–80%). geom_text + position_stack labels stacked in the wrong order until an explicit group was set; “100%” collided with the next panel’s “0%” until panel.spacing.x was widened. p_fmt(x, 0) NA gotcha hit again in summary.qmd (second argument is accuracy).

Nothing committed; r/pums/, profiles.qmd, summary.qmd, and data-out/pums_*.csv are untracked.

title: LOG.md — dev log
text:
What changed: Added r/pep_migration.R (user request): PEP births, deaths, natural change, international and domestic migration for the 17 rr localities, pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17, and Virginia. Source is the Census co-est2019-alldata.csv (2010–2019) and co-est2025-alldata.csv (2020–2025) files, cached under data/cache/pep/. Outputs data/pep_migration.rds (annual + era frames) and two CSVs. Added three H2 sections to demographics.qmd after the population-growth section (4 figures, 1 table, a callout), plus a migration bullet in the closing summary. Documented the vintage and partial-year rules in METHODOLOGY.md.
Design decisions: The files are used instead of tidycensus::get_estimates() because the API returns only a vintage’s latest year (probed: vintage 2025 → year 2025 only), so a series from it would mix revised and unrevised vintages. The two vintages don’t join — the 2019 → 2020 regional step (1,291,900 → 1,316,683) spans the 2020 Census rebase — so annual change is never computed across it and the page compares eras. The 2010 and 2020 components are April–June only (Richmond city births: 765 in 2020 vs. 2,872 in 2021) and are NA. Ran the script myself (two cached CSVs plus one tiny API call, ~7 s) since it isn’t a long pull.
Data surprises:

Natural increase collapsed; migration didn’t. Region: natural change 38,050 over 2011–2019 (4,228/yr) vs. 7,254 over 2021–2025 (1,451/yr); net migration 65,684 (7,298/yr) vs. 65,176 (13,035/yr). Migration share of growth 63% → 90%. 10 of 17 localities had more deaths than births in 2020–2025.
Region outgrew Virginia in 13 of 14 years (all but 2011). 2024 was the peak at +1.47% (19,910 people), driven by a record 10,787 international migrants.
Richmond city flipped. Domestic net migration +5.3 → −1.1 per 1,000/yr; international 2.8 → 6.8. Henrico’s domestic is negative in both eras (−0.5, −3.1). Chesterfield and the expansion ring are domestic-driven; the ring’s net rate is 18.8/1,000/yr with negative natural change (migration share 106%).
14 of 17 localities had a higher net migration rate in the 2020s; Henrico, Prince George, and Richmond city did not. New Kent (36.6) and Goochland (35.2) lead.
Validation: all component identities hold exactly in both files (Δpop = natural + net migration + residual; net = international + domestic); rr17 reconciles to its 17 members in all 16 years; 2025 population and net migration match the Census API (Vintage 2025) for all 17 localities.
Bugs caught: p_fmt(x, 0) — its second argument is accuracy, not digits — rendered a title as “Migration supplied NA of growth” (fixed to 1); formattable::percent() can’t mix with a character in if_else(). The shell also choked on a long heredoc, so the page patch ran from a script file.
