profiles.qmd reads household-level 2020-2024 ACS PUMS. The r/pums/ scripts run in this order: rva_puma.R (PUMA lookup), pums_collect.R (pull), pums_ami.R (assigns each household an AMI band), pums_profiles.R (tidy estimates the page reads). pums_prep.R (with naics_soc_lookup.R and the data-out/puma_pow.csv place-of-work crosswalk) builds a person-level recoded file, data/pums_rva.rds; nothing reads it yet.

profiles.qmd covers the core three only (changed 2026-10-30). BHC’s target population is Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield, so pums_profiles.R keeps only puma_core3 (Chesterfield ×3, Henrico ×2, Richmond city ×2), which tile those localities exactly. The two mixed PUMAs (08501, 14501) stay in the raw pull and rva_ami_pums.rds but are dropped before estimation. Totals are core-three totals (381,842 households, 924,266 residents) and will not match the 17-locality ACS tables; never present them side by side without saying so.
AMI bands. HUD FY2026 Richmond income limits (data/summary_county_5176099999.csv, MFI $113,500) applied by household size to every PUMA in the pull (capped at 8). 30/50/80% are HUD’s; 60/100/120% are derived from the 50% limit. Household income is inflated ADJINC → 2024 dollars → 2026 dollars (CPI-U, Jan-Sep 2026 / 2024 average = 332.243 / 313.689) so it compares with FY2026 limits. Zero- and negative-income households are folded into the “30% AMI or less” profile band and counted in the callout.
Vacant units and group quarters (TEN == "b") are excluded; their missing income would otherwise land in the top band.
Standard errors use the 80 replicate weights, sqrt(4/80 * sum((rep - est)^2)). Reliability reuses flag_reliability() on the CV of each estimate; shares of small categories are noisier than counts, so the page suppresses Low cells in tables and shows all in the stacked bars.
Benchmark. pums_profiles.R checks PUMS owner and renter households in puma_core3 against ACS B25003 for bhc (same 2020-2024 window), 3% tolerance (observed within 0.6%).












Source
Vintage in use




ACS 5-year
Three non-overlapping 5-year windows ending 2014, 2019, 2024 — the trend convention acs_tenure.R set and acs_stock.R follows. Overlapping 5-year samples are not independent, so the site never plots consecutive windows against each other. Check acs_burden.R’s header for its own vintage


tigris boundaries
2023 cartographic boundary (500k), per r/geo.R


BPS permits
See r/bps_permits.R’s header


PEP county estimates
Two vintages that do not join: Vintage 2019 (2010–2019) and Vintage 2025 (2020–2025), from the Census co-est*-alldata.csv files cached under data/cache/pep/. See r/pep_migration.R’s header






acs_stock.R covers B25001 (total units), B25002 (occupancy), B25004 (vacancy status), B25024 (units in structure), B25034 (year built), and B25035 (median year built). B25036 (year built by tenure) is out of scope for v1 — it is not published in the 2014 window, which would break the three-window trend every other frame in that script carries. B25035 is a median and cannot be summed, so unlike the other frames it carries no pooled bhc3/secondary4 rows.
Pooled rows. Frames that hold counts carry two synthetic geographies alongside the published ones: bhc3 (the 3 core localities) and secondary4 (the 4 expansion localities). Counts add and MOEs combine in quadrature, both computed in the r/ script so pages only filter and plot. Ashland sits inside Hanover and is therefore never pooled — doing so would double-count it.
pep_migration.R (PEP components of change). Never join the two vintages: Vintage 2020+ is built on the 2020 Census base, so the 2019 → 2020 population step spans a methodology break and is not computed — each of the two eras (2010–2019, 2020–2025) is summarized inside one vintage. The 2010 and 2020 components cover only April 1 – June 30 and are set to NA (population is kept). The files, not tidycensus::get_estimates(), are the source because the API returns only a vintage’s latest year. Rates are per 1,000 over the average of start- and end-year population. No Ashland (PEP has no sub-county components) and no comparison metros (CBSA delineations differ across the two vintages). Pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17 and Virginia are plain sums — PEP counts are administrative estimates with no MOE. PEP and ACS growth rates measure different periods with different methods and are never compared directly.
cache_table = TRUE is now a no-op: current tidycensus deprecates it in favor of Census API groups and warns once per call. Harmless, and CLAUDE.md still prescribes it, so scripts keep passing it; drop it project-wide in a dedicated cleanup rather than piecemeal.

Keep this table current as scripts are added — it’s the fastest way for a session to know what year’s data is actually on the site without opening every script.





Public data only. No MLS, no CoStar, no CHAS, no PUMS-based gap analysis for v1. Everything here comes from a package (tidycensus, tigris) or a public government file server.
Three pages, not five. The sibling project this repo’s early docs were copied from split market data into ownership.qmd + rental.qmd; this project combines that into one market.qmd, matching the simpler three-area scope (inventory / demographics / market).
No reliability gate on the bhc core. flag_reliability() is reserved for secondary and ashland estimates, where small populations push CVs up. The 3-locality core is large enough that this isn’t usually needed, but check CVs before assuming that on any new table.




Two prior docs in this repo (an earlier CLAUDE.md/TODO.md pair, and a PLAN.md) described a materially larger project — PUMS gap analysis, CHAS tables, MLS/CoStar pipelines, a 5-chapter book, vulnerable-populations data — that was never actually built here. Those docs were copied from a sibling Richmond-nonprofit engagement and a separate Fauquier County study, respectively, and rewritten on 2026-09-15 to match what actually exists in this repo. If a future session finds a stray reference to pha, puma_core3-driven chapters, r/chas.R, r/mls_*, or Fauquier/Better Housing Coalition anywhere, it’s leftover — flag it rather than trusting it.

title: Housing need in the Richmond region
section: The region is growing, and migration is doing the work
text:
The region is growing, and migration is doing the work



10.7% population growth, 17-locality region, 2014 to 2024 windows


1,341,248 people live in the region today


90% of regional growth, 2020-2025, comes from new people moving into the region













This is context, not the argument. Population is up across the region and more of that growth now depends on people moving in, which is why housing supply and cost matter to the region’s future. Chesterfield and the expansion ring grew fastest. Richmond city has shifted toward international in-migration.

title: Housing need in the Richmond region
section: About 84,000 renter households earn 80% of AMI or less
text:
About 84,000 renter households earn 80% of AMI or less



84,000 City and surrounding county renter households at or below 80% of area median income (AMI): 60% of renters


81% of renters at 30% of AMI or less pay half or more of income on housing













AMI is area median income, using HUD limits for the Richmond area. The core three are Richmond city, Henrico and Chesterfield. Need is deepest at the bottom: most of the lowest-income renters pay half or more of income on housing. The top band is a small sample, so don’t quote it.

title: Housing need in the Richmond region
section: Home values rose far faster than renter incomes
text:
Home values rose far faster than renter incomes

title: Housing need in the Richmond region
section: Tenants: three bills on mold, fees and deposits
text:
Tenants: three bills on mold, fees and deposits


HB79, mold. Lets tenants sue for damages, including punitive damages and attorney fees, when mold results solely from a landlord’s gross negligence or willful misconduct. Requires temporary vacating for remediation when a physician certifies a health risk.
HB1409, rental agreement fees. Bars agreements that charge tenants for building maintenance, pest control, trash, common-area utilities or security, or for internet and cable above the landlord’s cost.
SB349, pre-tenancy fees. Limits landlords to defined pre-tenancy fees, requires written notice of them before collecting anything, and limits how security and pet deposits can be applied.



All three amend the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. HB79 and HB1409 were continued to 2027 in House General Laws, and in 2026 a subcommittee recommended continuing each to 2028, so watch whether either gets a hearing. These are summaries from LIS, not legal analysis.

title: Housing need in the Richmond region
section: Land use: five bills on approvals and public land
text:
Land use: five bills on approvals and public land


HB419, approval deadlines. Every locality must approve, approve with conditions, or deny a residential rezoning or development application within 12 months.
SB717, transit-oriented overlays. Requires six stories and 30 units per acre by right near major transit stops, ministerial approval, effective September 2027 with a 2030 sunset. Passed the Senate in 2026.
HB143, surplus property. Offers suitable state surplus land to affordable housing developers for at least 90 days, with a 30-year affordability covenant; localities inventory their own land.
HB1376, redevelopment fund. Removes the $500,000 cap and the 100% local match on the Urban Public-Private Partnership Redevelopment Fund.
HB464, accessory dwelling units. Directs the state housing department to publish a construction guide with local rules and model designs.



SB717 is the most far-reaching. As passed by the Senate it covers certain localities, allows some areas to be excluded, and ends September 1, 2030. HB419 was continued in House Counties, Cities and Towns, with a subcommittee recommending continuing it to 2028.

Acquisition Fund pilot (budget request). A three-year revolving loan program run by the state housing department to buy and preserve units at affordable rates, for localities with a right-of-first-refusal ordinance that match state dollars.



HB183 is a savings-account bill; it helps households that can already save, so pair it with the renter-income numbers earlier in the deck. The tax credit change and the acquisition pilot are not filed yet, and the pilot’s dollar amount is not set.

title: Summary
section: The region is growing, and migration is doing the work
text:
The region is growing, and migration is doing the work

The region grew 10.7% to 1,341,248 people, led by Chesterfield (16.5%) and the four-locality expansion ring (15.5%); Richmond city grew 8.7% and Henrico 6.6%.
Natural increase fell from 4,228 people a year in 2010-2019 to 1,451 in 2020-2025, so net migration now supplies 90% of growth. In 10 of the 17 localities deaths exceeded births over 2020-2025.
International migration peaked at 10,787 in 2024; the latest year, 2025, was 5,387.
Richmond city flipped from domestic to international growth: its international migration rate rose from 2.8 to 6.8 per 1,000 a year while its domestic rate went from +5.3 to -1.1.







Full detail: Demographics

title: Summary
section: The population is older, more diverse, and more often living alone
text:
The population is older, more diverse, and more often living alone

The 65-and-over share rose from 12.9% to 16.7% while the under-18 share fell from 22.7% to 21.3%. The expansion ring is oldest at 20.0%.
The Hispanic or Latino share rose from 5.5% to 8.4%, and the White non-Hispanic share fell from 58.7% to 54.7%. Richmond city moved the other way: its White share rose from 39.7% to 41.4%.
43.1% of Richmond city households are one person, against 61.4% married-couple families in the expansion ring. Region-wide, 29.6% of households are one person.
Real median household income in the Richmond MSA rose 9.6% to $86,679. Renters are far behind: their median household income was $54,728 (up 14.1%), and 45.9% of renter households earn under $50,000, against 18.9% of owners.







Full detail: Demographics

title: Summary
section: The housing stock is single-family, older in the city, and built out in the suburbs
text:
The housing stock is single-family, older in the city, and built out in the suburbs

The three core localities held 404,918 housing units, up 13.3%; the expansion ring grew 18.4% from a much smaller base.
Single-family detached homes are 63% of the core’s stock and 88% of the ring’s. Only Richmond city is substantially multifamily (22% of units in buildings of 20 or more).
38% of Richmond city’s housing predates 1950, against 2% in Chesterfield.
Vacancy is tight in the suburbs (3.8% in Chesterfield, 5.7% across the core) and highest in the southern localities (Sussex and Petersburg lead).
Permitting bottomed at 2,520 units in 2011, reached a series high of 10,414 in 2022, and was 9,091 in 2025. Multifamily outnumbered single-family permits in 3 of the last 4 years, and was 52% of 2025 units.







Full detail: Inventory

title: Summary
section: Home values rose faster than renter incomes; renters are no better off
text:
Home values rose faster than renter incomes; renters are no better off

After inflation, the Richmond MSA’s median home value rose 24.1% and median gross rent 11.3%, against 14.1% for median renter household income (the rent and renter-income changes are within each other’s margins of error; the home-value change is not). All-household median income rose 9.6%.
The typical home was worth 5.9 times the typical renter household income in the 2014 window and 6.5 times in 2024. Median rent equalled 31.7% of median renter income, from 32.5%.
Renter cost burden has not eased: 51.2% of renter households pay 30% or more of income on housing (51.4% in 2014), and 25.7% pay half or more. Owner burden fell from 26.1% to 20.0%.
Renter burden is now nearly identical across the core: 52.0% in Richmond city, 51.6% in Henrico, 52.2% in Chesterfield.
Ownership held near two-thirds (67.0%). Richmond city is the only core locality where renters outnumber owners (58,914 renter households to 45,407).







Full detail: Market

title: Summary
section: Evictions have not fully rebounded, and lending has settled below its 2021 peak
text:
Evictions have not fully rebounded, and lending has settled below its 2021 peak

Eviction filings in the core three fell from 37,548 in 2016 to 7,575 in 2021 (80% lower), then recovered to 31,520 in 2025.
The latest 12 months run at 85% of the historical average, 15% below the 2016-19 monthly mean. Richmond city is furthest below baseline (81%) and Chesterfield closest (97%).
Home-purchase loans originated for principal residences peaked at 17,262 in 2021, fell to 10,607 in 2023, and were 10,877 in 2025. Counting refinances, the swings are larger (49,661 in 2021, 20,984 in 2025).
The home-purchase denial rate was 8.3% in 2025, against 8.2% in 2018. Over the last four years Black applicants were denied 16.1% of the time and Hispanic or Latino applicants 10.6%, against 4.5% for non-Hispanic White applicants.
Across all denied applications (all loan purposes, not only home purchase, 2022-2025), debt-to-income (35.8%) and credit history (32.9%) are the most-cited denial reasons.







Full detail: Market. Eviction and lending figures cover Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield only. Filings are landlord court requests, not completed evictions, and the 2020-21 trough reflects pandemic moratoria and rental assistance. Lending counts cover one- to four-unit principal residences.

title: Summary
section: Lower-income renters carry the cost burden, and most live in Henrico and Chesterfield
text:
Lower-income renters carry the cost burden, and most live in Henrico and Chesterfield

40.2% of households in the core three earn 80% of area median income (AMI) or less: 60.3% of renters and 28.7% of owners.
Richmond city has the highest share (50.9%, against 39.1% in Henrico and 33.4% in Chesterfield), but only 44.6% of the core three’s lower-income renter households live in the city.
80.8% of renters at 30% of AMI or less pay half or more of income on housing, and 62.0% of renters at 51-80% of AMI pay 30% or more; above 120% of AMI, about 3% do (a small sample).
The lowest-income renters are mostly people living alone (58.5%) and are 55.9% Black; the lowest-income owners skew old (52.9% are 65 or over).







Full detail: Profiles. These figures come from household-level survey data (PUMS) for Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield only, not the 17 localities used elsewhere on this page.

title: Summary
section: What to watch
text:
What to watch






Seven things to look out for




Growth leans on migration. With natural increase down to 1,451 a year, a slowdown in international or domestic moves would show up directly in population growth. International migration in 2025 was 50% of its 2024 peak.
Home values are outrunning renter incomes. Real home values rose 24.1% against 14.1% for renter household income, and the value-to-renter-income ratio widened from 5.9 to 6.5. The value measure is every owner’s own estimate, so it understates the cost of buying today.
Half of renters are cost-burdened, and the gap by income is wide. The share did not improve over the decade, and the typical renter household earns far less than the typical owner household.
Production is volatile and its mix keeps changing. Permits swing between single-family and multifamily from year to year, and the expansion ring continues to build almost entirely detached homes (88% of its stock) even though 30% of the region’s households are one person.
Lower-income renters are where the burden concentrates. Renters at 30% of AMI or less number 30,599 households in the core three, and 80.8% of them pay half or more of income on housing.
The outer suburbs are the oldest part of the region. The expansion ring has the highest 65-and-over share (20.0%) and, in aggregate, more deaths than births in 2020-2025 (-1,058), so its growth depends entirely on in-migration.
Access to credit is uneven, and eviction filings are recovering but still below their old level. Black applicants were denied home-purchase loans 3.6 times as often as non-Hispanic White applicants, and eviction filings in the latest 12 months were at 85% of the historical average, after a trough of 7,575 filings in 2021.

Affordable rental housing

The core three have about 84,000 renter households at or below 80% of AMI, the income range where affordable rental housing is aimed. That is 60.3% of all renters, against 28.7% of owners.
Need is deepest at the bottom: 80.8% of renters at or below 30% of AMI pay half or more of their income on housing, and 62.0% of renters at 51-80% of AMI pay 30% or more. Above 120% of AMI, about 3% do (a small sample, so quote it loosely).
The burden is not easing region-wide: 51.2% of renter households pay 30% or more (51.4% in 2014), and real median rent rose 11.3% (±1.3 pts) while real median renter income rose 14.1% (±3.6 pts); those two changes are within each other’s margins of error, so do not say rent grew faster than renter income.
Housing stability is part of the case: filings in the core three are back to 85% of the historical average, about 2,600 a month, after falling to 7,575 for all of 2021. Filings are court requests, not completed evictions.
Where the need is: 55.4% of the core three’s lower-income renter households live in Henrico or Chesterfield, not Richmond city, even though the city has the highest share of lower-income households (50.9%).



Senior affordable housing

The region’s 65-and-over population grew from 12.9% to 16.7% of residents between the 2014 and 2024 windows, so the group BHC’s 8 senior properties serve is growing as a share of the region.
About 12,000 renter households in the core three have a householder 65 or over and income at or below 50% of AMI, 23% of all renter households in that range.
Older owners are exposed too: 52.9% of owner households at or below 30% of AMI have a householder 65 or over, roughly 17,500 older owner households at or below 50% of AMI.
The outer suburbs are the oldest part of the region (20.0% aged 65 and over in the expansion ring), with more deaths than births in 2020-2025, which points to a long-run need for senior housing outside the core.



Homeownership

The typical home was worth 5.9 times the typical renter household income in the 2014 window and 6.5 times in 2024; real median home value rose 24.1% against 14.1% for renter income.
About 70,000 owner households in the core three earn 80% of AMI or less (28.7% of owners), and 45.9% of renter households region-wide earn under $50,000, against 18.9% of owners. The gap between the two groups is the gap affordable homeownership has to bridge.
Access to credit is uneven: over 2022-2025, Black applicants were denied home-purchase loans 16.1% of the time and Hispanic or Latino applicants 10.6%, against 4.5% for non-Hispanic White applicants.
Across all denied applications (all loan purposes, 2022-2025; most denials in the lending data are refinance, cash-out, and home-improvement loans, so do not describe these as home-purchase denial reasons), debt-to-income (35.8%) and credit history (32.9%) lead, ahead of collateral and cash to close.
Lenders originated 10,877 home-purchase loans for principal residences in the core three in 2025, 37% below the 2021 peak of 17,262.



Mixed-income, mixed-use development

Richmond city is the one core locality where renters outnumber owners (58,914 renter households to 45,407) and the only one that is substantially multifamily, with 22% of units in buildings of 20 or more.
The suburbs are built almost entirely as detached homes: 63% of the core’s stock and 88% of the expansion ring’s, even though 30% of the region’s households are one person.
Production leans on multifamily in recent years: it outnumbered single-family permits in 3 of the last 4 years and was 52% of 2025 permitted units. Permits swing between 2,520 (2011) and 10,414 (2022) units a year.
Lower-income households are spread across the core, not concentrated in one place: 50.9% of households in Richmond city, 39.1% in Henrico, and 33.4% in Chesterfield are at or below 80% of AMI. That supports mixed-income communities in all three localities, not only in the city.
The region’s housing stock is old in the city (38% of Richmond city’s housing predates 1950) and tight in the suburbs (3.8% vacancy in Chesterfield), which limits the supply of affordable options without new construction.







Using these figures in communications




These are regional figures, not BHC results. They describe need and market conditions across Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield (or the 17-locality region where noted). They do not count BHC’s residents, properties, or outcomes; pair them with BHC’s own program data.
Say “at or below 80% of AMI,” not “low-income,” without a definition. AMI bands here follow HUD income limits for the Richmond area; see Profiles.
PUMS counts are survey estimates. Household counts by income band carry sampling error, so quote them rounded (for example, “about 31,000 renter households at or below 30% of AMI”).
Senior counts are PUMS survey estimates. They are weighted counts of households with a householder 65 or over (509 sample households for renters at or below 50% of AMI, margin of error ±1,100), so quote them as “about” and round to the nearest 500.
Lending rates are not sampled, but have caveats. HMDA counts reporting lenders’ applications, so the margin shown is only case-count noise. Denial rates exclude withdrawn and incomplete applications; about 16% of decided applications have no race or ethnicity recorded; lenders under the reporting threshold are not in the data.
The eviction baseline is the provider’s. The “percent of the historical average” has no documented definition. Prefer the count-based comparison (15% below the 2016-19 monthly mean) for anything external.
Check the wording of changes. Home values rose far faster than renter incomes (outside the margins of error); rent and renter-income changes are statistically similar.
The data do not measure demand for mixed-use space. The mixed-income points rest on income, tenure, and structure-type patterns; retail and commercial demand needs separate evidence.
Eviction filings are not evictions. Lead with the trend against the pre-2020 baseline, not a count of displaced households.









Reading the numbers




Stock and production are different series. Stock (ACS) counts units standing; production (Building Permits Survey) counts permits issued, which lead completions and can be cancelled.
Small geographies are noisy. The four expansion-ring localities and Ashland carry wide margins of error; the pages suppress cells with a coefficient of variation above 30.
Income-band figures use a different geography. They come from PUMS, which reports only whole PUMAs; the seven used here tile Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield exactly. The other localities are not covered, so these totals will not match the 17-locality pages.
Eviction and lending figures cover the core three only. Eviction filings are court records and lending figures are HMDA loan-level data; neither is ACS, so they will not reconcile with the 17-locality pages. Denial rates count denied / (originated + approved-not-accepted + denied) and are shown only where at least 100 applications were decided.
Migration figures are modeled from administrative records and revised each vintage. The 2010-2019 and 2020-2025 series come from different vintages and are compared, not joined.
Dollar changes are inflation-adjusted with national CPI-U, so they measure change relative to national prices, not a local cost-of-living index.
